rx-basics-001.explanation:
**What it is:** A regular expression is a small pattern language for describing text. Instead of writing loops to inspect characters one by one, you declare a pattern ("a digit, then two letters") and let the regex engine do the matching.

**In JavaScript:** A regex is a real object of type `RegExp`. You hand it to string methods (`match`, `replace`, `split`, `search`) or call its own methods (`test`, `exec`). The four jobs you'll use it for: **test** (does it match?), **find/extract** (pull out matches), **replace** (rewrite text), and **split** (break a string apart).

**Why learn it:** validation (emails, ZIP codes), parsing (logs, dates), and search-and-replace are everywhere. A one-line regex often replaces a dozen lines of manual string code.

rx-basics-002.explanation:
**The two ways:** A **literal** sits between slashes: `/abc/`. The **constructor** takes a string: `new RegExp('abc')`. Both produce an identical `RegExp` object.

**When to use the literal:** the pattern is fixed and known when you write the code. It's compiled once when the script is parsed, and it reads cleanly because you don't double-escape backslashes.

**When to use the constructor:** the pattern is dynamic — built from a variable, user input, or assembled at runtime. The catch: because the argument is a normal string, backslashes must be doubled (`'\\d'` to mean `\d`), since the string parser eats one layer first.

**Flags:** the literal takes them after the closing slash (`/abc/gi`); the constructor takes them as a second string argument (`new RegExp('abc', 'gi')`).

rx-basics-mcq-001.explanation:
**Why the constructor:** When the pattern lives in a variable, only `new RegExp(variable)` reads the variable's *value*. A literal like `/word/i` is taken character-for-character — it matches the four letters w-o-r-d, never the contents of a variable named `word`.

**Where flags go:** the second argument. `new RegExp(word, 'i')` builds a case-insensitive matcher from whatever string `word` holds.

**A real gotcha — escaping user input:** if the variable comes from a user and might contain regex metacharacters (like `.` or `(`), build it carefully or escape it first, or the pattern will misbehave. The constructor does not escape for you.

rx-basics-003.explanation:
**What `g` does:** the global flag tells the engine to keep going after the first match and find them all.

**Effect per method:** with `match`, you get an array of every match instead of just the first; with `replace`/`replaceAll`, every occurrence is rewritten instead of only the first; `matchAll` actually *requires* `g`.

**The hidden side effect:** a global regex is **stateful** — it tracks a `lastIndex` property and advances it on each `exec`/`test` call. That's powerful for looping but causes surprising bugs if you reuse one global regex across separate `test` calls (see the `lastIndex` gotcha card).

rx-basics-004.explanation:
**What `i` does:** case-insensitive matching. With it, `/cat/i` matches `cat`, `Cat`, `CAT`, `cAt`, and so on.

**Why it matters:** without `i`, regex is case-sensitive by default, so user-facing search and validation often need it. It's cheap and very common.

**Combine flags freely:** flags stack in any order — `/cat/gi` is global *and* case-insensitive. For non-ASCII letters (é, Ω), pair `i` with the `u` (unicode) flag for correct case folding.
rx-basics-004.example:
```js
console.log(/cat/.test('A CAT'));  // false (case-sensitive)
console.log(/cat/i.test('A CAT')); // true

// Stacking flags: case-insensitive + global
const found = 'Cat cat CAT'.match(/cat/gi);
console.log(found); // ['Cat', 'cat', 'CAT']
```

rx-basics-mcq-002.explanation:
**What `m` changes:** it only affects the anchors `^` and `$`. Normally `^` means start-of-string and `$` means end-of-string. With `m`, they mean start-of-line and end-of-line, so they also match right after / before each `\n`.

**The classic confusion:** `m` does NOT make `.` match newlines — that's the separate `s` (dotAll) flag. Many people mix these up.

**Where it's useful:** processing multi-line text (a textarea, a file's contents) line by line with a single regex, e.g. matching every line that starts with `#`.

rx-basics-mr-001.explanation:
**The full set:** JavaScript has exactly seven regex flags — `g` (global), `i` (ignoreCase), `m` (multiline), `s` (dotAll: `.` matches newlines), `u` (unicode), `y` (sticky: match only at `lastIndex`), and `d` (hasIndices: record start/end positions of each capture).

**Not JavaScript flags:** `x` (the extended/verbose mode that ignores whitespace and allows comments) exists in PCRE/Python/Java but NOT in JS. `z` isn't a flag in any common engine. Knowing what *doesn't* exist saves you from copying patterns from other languages that silently break.

**Reading them back:** `regex.flags` returns the active flags as a string, and there are boolean accessors like `regex.global`.

rx-char-001.explanation:
**What `\d` matches:** any single digit. It's shorthand for the character class `[0-9]`.

**The opposite:** `\D` matches any single character that is NOT a digit (a letter, space, punctuation).

**One token = one character:** `\d` matches *one* digit. To match several, add a quantifier: `\d+` (one or more), `\d{4}` (exactly four). A four-digit year is `\d{4}`.

**Unicode note:** by default `\d` is only `0-9`. It does not match other numeral systems unless you opt into special unicode property escapes.
rx-char-001.example:
```js
console.log(/\d/.test('abc7')); // true (there is a digit)
console.log(/\d/.test('abc'));  // false

// One digit vs many
console.log('id 2026'.match(/\d/g));   // ['2','0','2','6'] one at a time
console.log('id 2026'.match(/\d+/g));  // ['2026'] a whole run

// \D — non-digits
console.log('a1b2'.match(/\D/g)); // ['a', 'b']
```

rx-char-002.explanation:
**What `\w` matches:** a single 'word' character — a letter, a digit, or an underscore. It's exactly `[A-Za-z0-9_]`.

**What it does NOT match:** spaces, punctuation, hyphens, or (by default) accented/non-ASCII letters like `é` or `ñ`. The name 'word character' is a bit misleading because of the underscore-yes / accent-no rules.

**The opposite:** `\W` matches any non-word character.

**Common use:** `\w+` grabs identifiers or simple words. If you need real Unicode letters, use the `u` flag with a Unicode property escape like `\p{L}` instead.

rx-char-003.explanation:
**What `\s` matches:** any single whitespace character — a regular space, tab (`\t`), newline (`\n`), carriage return (`\r`), form feed, and a few Unicode spaces.

**The opposite:** `\S` matches any non-whitespace character.

**Where it shines:** normalising or splitting text. `\s+` matches a run of whitespace, so `str.split(/\s+/)` breaks a string into words regardless of how many spaces/tabs separate them, and `str.replace(/\s+/g, ' ')` collapses messy whitespace to single spaces.

rx-char-004.explanation:
**What the dot matches:** any single character — except a line terminator (`\n`, `\r`, …) by default.

**Match a literal dot:** escape it as `\.`. This is the single most common regex mistake — an unescaped dot in something like `3.14` or `file.txt` matches *any* character, not the period.

**The `s` (dotAll) flag:** add it and `.` will also match newlines, which is what you want when scanning across multiple lines.

**Be specific when you can:** `.*` is a blunt instrument; a tighter class like `[^,]*` (anything but a comma) is often safer and faster than a wildcard.

rx-char-mcq-001.explanation:
**Negated class:** inside square brackets, a `^` as the *first* character flips the meaning — `[^aeiou]` matches any one character that is NOT a, e, i, o, or u.

**Context for `^`:** the same symbol means two different things depending on where it sits. At the start of a class (`[^...]`) it negates; outside a class it's the start-of-string anchor. Position decides.

**Still one character:** a negated class still matches exactly one character. `[^aeiou]+` would match a run of non-vowels.

**A literal `^`:** to match an actual caret inside a class, put it anywhere but first, e.g. `[a^]`.

rx-char-mcq-002.explanation:
**Ranges:** a hyphen between two characters inside a class defines a range based on character codes. `[a-z]` is every lowercase letter, `[A-Z]` uppercase, `[0-9]` digits.

**Combine ranges:** put several in one class — `[A-Za-z0-9]` matches any alphanumeric. Order doesn't matter; `[0-9A-F]` is hex digits.

**Literal hyphen:** to match an actual `-`, put it first or last in the class (`[-a-z]` or `[a-z-]`) or escape it (`[a\-z]`). A hyphen in the middle is interpreted as a range.

**Why not just `.`:** a class is precise. `[a-z]` rejects digits and symbols; the dot accepts almost anything.

rx-anchor-001.explanation:
**Anchors match positions, not characters:** `^` asserts 'we are at the start of the string' and `$` asserts 'we are at the end'. They consume no characters.

**Why they're essential for validation:** without anchors, a pattern can match a fragment buried inside a larger string. `/\d{5}/` matches the `12345` inside `abc12345xyz`; `/^\d{5}$/` only matches when the *entire* string is five digits.

**With the `m` flag:** `^` and `$` switch to start/end of each line instead of the whole string.

**Mental model:** wrap a validation pattern in `^...$` to mean 'the whole input must look exactly like this'.
rx-anchor-001.example:
```js
// Anchored: the WHOLE string must be 'cat'
console.log(/^cat$/.test('cat'));     // true
console.log(/^cat$/.test('cats'));    // false
console.log(/^cat$/.test('a cat'));   // false

// Unanchored: matches 'cat' anywhere inside
console.log(/cat/.test('a cat sat')); // true
```

rx-anchor-mcq-001.explanation:
**Reading `^\d+$`:** start of string, then one-or-more digits, then end of string. In plain English: 'the entire string is nothing but digits (at least one)'.

**Why the others fail:** `'12a45'` contains a letter, so the run of digits can't reach `$`. `'  123'` has leading spaces before the first digit, so it can't start at `^`. `'12.5'` has a dot, which `\d` doesn't match.

**Takeaway:** anchoring turns a 'contains' check into an 'is exactly' check — the difference between `test`ing a substring and validating a whole field.
rx-anchor-mcq-001.example:
```js
const isAllDigits = (s) => /^\d+$/.test(s);

console.log(isAllDigits('12345')); // true
console.log(isAllDigits('12a45')); // false (letter)
console.log(isAllDigits('  123')); // false (spaces)
console.log(isAllDigits('12.5'));  // false (dot)
console.log(isAllDigits(''));      // false (+ needs >= 1)
```

rx-anchor-002.explanation:
**What `\b` is:** a word-boundary assertion. It matches the empty position between a word character (`\w`) and a non-word character (or the string edge). Like `^`/`$`, it matches a *position*, not a character.

**Why it's useful:** it lets you match whole words. `/\bcat\b/` matches `cat` in `'a cat sat'` but not the `cat` inside `'category'` or `'scatter'`, because those neighbours are word characters.

**The inverse:** `\B` matches a non-boundary — a position *between* two word characters or two non-word characters. `/\Bcat\B/` would match `cat` inside `'scatter'`.

**Gotcha:** `\b` is based on `\w`, so it treats `_` as part of a word and treats accented letters as boundaries by default.

rx-quant-001.explanation:
**The three basic quantifiers:** they say how many times the *preceding token* may repeat. `*` = zero or more, `+` = one or more, `?` = zero or one (i.e. optional).

**Applies to one token:** `a+` repeats the single `a`. To repeat a group, wrap it: `(ab)+` matches `ab`, `abab`, …

**`*` vs `+`:** the difference is whether 'none' counts. `a*` happily matches an empty string; `a+` needs at least one `a`. That makes `+` the right choice when something must be present.

**Greedy by default:** all three grab as much as they can before backtracking — see the greedy-vs-lazy card.
rx-quant-001.example:
```js
console.log(/a+/.test(''));   // false (needs >= 1)
console.log(/a*/.test(''));   // true  (0 is allowed)

// ? makes a token optional — match 'color' or 'colour'
console.log(/colou?r/.test('color'));  // true
console.log(/colou?r/.test('colour')); // true

// Quantifier on a group
console.log('ababab'.match(/(ab)+/)[0]); // 'ababab'
```

rx-quant-mcq-001.explanation:
**Exact count `{n}`:** `\d{3}` matches exactly three digits in a row — no more required, no fewer accepted at that spot.

**The family:** `{n}` exactly n, `{n,}` n or more, `{n,m}` between n and m inclusive. So `\d{2,4}` matches 2, 3, or 4 digits.

**No spaces inside braces:** `{2, 4}` (with a space) is not a valid quantifier in older engines and may be treated as literal text — write `{2,4}`.

**Pair with anchors for validation:** `^\d{3}$` insists the whole string is precisely three digits — useful for fixed-length codes.
rx-quant-mcq-001.example:
```js
const re = /^\d{3}$/; // exactly three digits, whole string
console.log(re.test('123'));  // true
console.log(re.test('12'));   // false (too few)
console.log(re.test('1234')); // false (too many)

// Range form {n,m}
console.log('1 22 333 4444'.match(/\d{2,3}/g)); // ['22','333','444']
```

rx-quant-mcq-002.explanation:
**Greedy means maximal:** by default `.*` matches as many characters as possible, then backtracks only as much as needed to let the rest of the pattern succeed. Against `<a><b>`, `<.*>` grabs everything up to the *last* `>`.

**The fix — lazy:** append `?` to make it lazy. `<.*?>` matches as little as possible, so it stops at the *first* `>` and returns `<a>`.

**The even-better fix — be specific:** `<[^>]*>` ('angle bracket, then anything that isn't a `>`, then `>`') avoids the greedy/lazy question entirely and is faster. Reaching for a precise character class beats wildcards in most parsing tasks.
rx-quant-mcq-002.example:
```js
const s = '<a><b>';

console.log(s.match(/<.*>/)[0]);   // '<a><b>'  greedy (to last >)
console.log(s.match(/<.*?>/)[0]);  // '<a>'     lazy  (to first >)
console.log(s.match(/<[^>]*>/)[0]); // '<a>'    specific, best

// All tags, lazily
console.log(s.match(/<.*?>/g)); // ['<a>', '<b>']
```

rx-quant-002.explanation:
**Making a quantifier lazy:** add `?` right after it. `*?`, `+?`, `??`, and `{2,5}?` are the lazy versions of `*`, `+`, `?`, and `{2,5}`. Lazy means 'match as few characters as possible while still allowing the overall pattern to succeed'.

**Why you'd want it:** when a greedy quantifier overshoots and swallows text you meant to stop at — the classic case is matching the *shortest* span between two delimiters.

**`.+?` idiom:** the go-to 'smallest possible chunk' pattern. But remember a precise character class (`[^x]+`) is usually clearer and faster than a lazy wildcard.

**Don't confuse the two `?`s:** the first `?` after a token is the optional quantifier; a `?` after *another* quantifier makes it lazy.

rx-group-001.explanation:
**Two jobs of parentheses:** (1) **grouping** — make a quantifier or alternation apply to several tokens at once, e.g. `(ab)+` or `(cat|dog)s`; (2) **capturing** — remember the text each group matched so you can read it back.

**Where captures show up:** in a `match`/`exec` result array at index `[1]`, `[2]`, … (index `[0]` is always the whole match); in `replace` as `$1`, `$2`; and as backreferences `\1` inside the pattern itself.

**Numbering:** groups are numbered by the order of their opening `(`, left to right.

**Don't need the capture?** use a non-capturing group `(?:...)` to group without filling the results array.

rx-group-mcq-001.explanation:
**The pipe `|` is OR:** `cat|dog` matches either `cat` or `dog`. It's called alternation.

**`|` has very low precedence:** it splits the *whole* pattern unless you scope it with a group. `^cat|dog$` actually means '(`^cat`) or (`dog$`)' — start-with-cat OR end-with-dog — almost never what you want.

**Scope it with parentheses:** `^(cat|dog)$` means the entire string is exactly `cat` or exactly `dog`. The group both bounds the alternation and (here) captures which one matched.

**Multiple options:** chain them — `(red|green|blue)`.

rx-group-002.explanation:
**Non-capturing group:** write `(?:...)`. It groups tokens — so a quantifier or `|` can apply to the whole thing — without saving the matched text as a numbered capture.

**Why bother:** (1) it keeps your capture numbers meaningful — only the groups you actually care about get `[1]`, `[2]`; (2) it's marginally more efficient because the engine doesn't record the substring; (3) it signals intent: 'I'm grouping for structure, not to extract'.

**Typical use:** wrapping an optional or repeated chunk you don't need to read back, e.g. an optional `https?://` prefix or repeated `(?:, \w+)*` list tails.

rx-group-003.explanation:
**Named capturing group:** write `(?<name>...)`. The matched text is then available on the result's `.groups` object as `match.groups.name`, in addition to its usual numeric index.

**Why use names:** captures become self-documenting. `match.groups.year` is far clearer than `match[1]`, and reordering the pattern won't silently shift your indices.

**In replacements:** reference a named group with `$<name>`, e.g. swap date parts with `$<day>/$<month>/$<year>`.

**Backreference by name:** inside the pattern, `\k<name>` matches the same text the named group captured.

rx-escape-001.explanation:
**Escaping:** many characters have special meaning in regex — `. * + ? ( ) [ ] { } ^ $ | \` and `/`. To match one literally, put a backslash in front: `\.` for a dot, `\(` for a parenthesis, `\\` for a backslash.

**The dot is the usual culprit:** an unescaped `.` matches any character, so `3.14` and `file.txt` patterns will match more than you intend until you escape the period.

**Inside a class, fewer escapes are needed:** most metacharacters are literal inside `[...]`, so `[.+]` matches a literal dot or plus.

**Escaping dynamic input:** when building a regex from a variable, escape regex-special characters first (manually, or with `RegExp.escape` where available) so user text like `a.b` isn't treated as a pattern.

rx-method-test-001.explanation:
**What `test` returns:** a boolean — `true` if the pattern matches anywhere in the string, `false` otherwise. It's a method *of the regex*, called as `regex.test(str)`.

**When to use it:** any yes/no question — 'is this a valid email shape?', 'does this contain a digit?'. It's the fastest option because the engine can stop at the first match and doesn't build a results array.

**Watch the global flag:** if the regex has `g` (or `y`), `test` becomes stateful and advances `lastIndex` between calls, which can make repeated calls alternate true/false. For a simple one-off check, don't use `g`.
rx-method-test-001.example:
```js
console.log(/\d/.test('abc4')); // true (contains a digit)
console.log(/\d/.test('abc'));  // false

// Validation read clearly
const isHex = (s) => /^[0-9a-f]+$/i.test(s);
console.log(isHex('1aF')); // true
console.log(isHex('1xF')); // false
```

rx-method-match-001.explanation:
**Without `g`, `match` returns rich detail about the FIRST match:** an array-like object where `[0]` is the matched text, `[1]`, `[2]`… are capture groups, plus properties `index` (where the match started), `input` (the original string), and `groups` (named captures, or `undefined`).

**Why this shape:** it mirrors `RegExp.prototype.exec` for a single match. The extra metadata is handy when you need to know *where* the match was, not just what it was.

**Contrast with `g`:** add the global flag and `match` throws away all that metadata, returning a plain array of matched strings (see the next card). Choose based on whether you need positions/captures.

rx-method-match-mcq-001.explanation:
**With `g`, `match` returns a flat array of all matched substrings:** `'a1b2c3'.match(/\d/g)` gives `['1','2','3']`. No `index`, no `input`, and crucially **no capture groups**.

**The trade-off:** global `match` is the quickest way to collect every match's *text*, but if your pattern has capture groups and you need them per match, this drops them — reach for `matchAll` instead.

**No-match result:** still `null`, not `[]` — guard before using the result.

**Mental rule:** `match` without `g` = one rich object; `match` with `g` = many plain strings.
rx-method-match-mcq-001.example:
```js
console.log('a1b2c3'.match(/\d/g)); // ['1', '2', '3']

// With g, capture groups are LOST — you only get full matches
console.log('a1b2'.match(/([a-z])(\d)/g)); // ['a1', 'b2'] (no [1]/[2])

// No match -> null (not [])
console.log('abc'.match(/\d/g)); // null
```

rx-method-match-002.explanation:
**The null gotcha:** when nothing matches, `String.prototype.match` returns `null` — not an empty array. This trips people up because the success case looks array-like.

**Why it bites:** code like `str.match(re).length` or `str.match(re)[0]` throws `TypeError: Cannot read properties of null` the moment there's no match. It's a common source of production crashes.

**How to guard:** check the result first (`const m = str.match(re); if (m) {...}`), or use optional chaining and a fallback (`str.match(re)?.[0] ?? ''`), or use `matchAll`/spread which yields an empty array on no match (`[...str.matchAll(re)]`).

rx-method-matchall-001.explanation:
**What `matchAll` returns:** an *iterator* of full match objects — each one shaped like a non-global `match`/`exec` result, with `[0]`, capture groups at `[1]`/`[2]`, `index`, `input`, and `groups`. So you keep per-match detail for *every* match.

**The `g` requirement:** the regex must include the global flag, or `matchAll` throws a `TypeError`. This is by design, to make the 'all matches' intent explicit.

**Consuming it:** it's an iterator, so spread it (`[...str.matchAll(re)]`) or `for...of` over it. You can't index it directly.

**Why prefer it over `match`/g:** `match` with `g` discards capture groups; `matchAll` is the modern, clean way to get groups for all matches without an `exec` loop.

rx-method-matchall-mcq-001.explanation:
**The key difference:** `match` with `g` returns only the matched *strings* and throws away each match's capture groups and index. `matchAll` returns a full match object per match, so you can read `m[1]`, `m.groups`, `m.index` for every one.

**When `match`/g is fine:** you only need the list of matched substrings (e.g. all numbers in a string).

**When you need `matchAll`:** your pattern captures sub-parts you want for each occurrence — key/value pairs, date components, every `<tag attr>` — and looping with positions matters.

**Bonus:** `matchAll` avoids the stateful `exec`-loop bug, because it manages `lastIndex` internally.

rx-method-replace-001.explanation:
**Default is first-only:** `String.prototype.replace` with a regex (no `g`) rewrites only the *first* match. `'a-b-c'.replace(/-/, '+')` → `'a+b-c'`.

**Replace everything:** add the `g` flag — `'a-b-c'.replace(/-/g, '+')` → `'a+b+c'`. This is the most common cause of 'why did only one get replaced?'.

**String vs regex argument:** if the first argument is a plain string (not a regex), `replace` also only replaces the first occurrence — that's what `replaceAll` exists to fix. With a regex, you control it with `g`.

**Returns a new string:** strings are immutable, so `replace` never mutates — assign or use the return value.

rx-method-replace-mcq-001.explanation:
**`$1` is a backreference in the replacement:** it inserts the text captured by the first capturing group. `$2` is the second group, and so on.

**The full set of replacement patterns:** `$&` = the whole match, `` $` `` = text before the match, `$'` = text after, `$<name>` = a named group, and `$$` = a literal dollar sign.

**Classic use — reorder captures:** swap 'First Last' to 'Last First' by capturing both words and emitting `$2 $1`.

**Only in the replacement string:** these `$n` forms are special only in `replace`'s second argument; inside the *pattern* the equivalent is `\1`.

rx-method-replace-002.explanation:
**Replacer function:** pass a function as the second argument and it's called once per match. Its return value becomes the replacement for that match.

**What it receives, in order:** the whole match, then each capture group (`g1`, `g2`, …), then the match's `offset` (index), then the full input string. If there are named groups, an object of them is passed as the final argument.

**Why use it:** when the replacement must be *computed* — uppercase a word, double a number, look a value up in a map — not just a static string.

**Returns are coerced to strings:** returning a number is fine; it gets stringified.

rx-method-replaceall-001.explanation:
**The rule:** if you pass a *regex* to `replaceAll`, it must carry the `g` flag — otherwise it throws a `TypeError`. This guards against the contradictory request 'replace all, but only the first match'.

**Why `replaceAll` exists:** `replace` with a plain *string* argument only swaps the first occurrence. `replaceAll` with a string swaps every occurrence — no regex needed, no escaping worries.

**Regex vs string argument:** use a string when you're matching literal text (`replaceAll(',', ';')`); use a global regex when you need a pattern (`replaceAll(/\s+/g, ' ')`).

**Same replacement features:** `$1`, `$&`, and replacer functions all work just like in `replace`.

rx-method-search-001.explanation:
**What `search` returns:** the index of the first match, or `-1` if there's no match. Think of it as `indexOf` but with a pattern instead of a literal substring.

**Boolean-ish use:** `str.search(re) !== -1` answers 'does it match?' — though `test` is the more direct tool for that.

**`g` is ignored:** `search` only ever reports the first match's position; the global flag has no effect.

**Position only:** it gives you *where*, not *what*. If you need the matched text or groups, use `match`/`exec` instead.

rx-method-split-001.explanation:
**Regex as a separator:** `String.prototype.split` accepts a regex, so the delimiter can be a *pattern* rather than a fixed string. `'a1b22c'.split(/\d+/)` splits at each run of digits → `['a','b','c']`.

**The killer use case — flexible whitespace:** `str.split(/\s+/)` splits into words no matter whether items are separated by one space, several, tabs, or newlines.

**Capturing groups are included:** if the separator regex has a capturing group, the captured delimiters are interleaved into the result array — sometimes handy, sometimes surprising.

**Edge cases:** a leading match produces an empty string at the start; `limit` (second arg) caps how many pieces you get.
rx-method-split-001.example:
```js
console.log('a1b22c'.split(/\d+/)); // ['a', 'b', 'c']

// Flexible whitespace splitting
console.log('one   two\tthree'.split(/\s+/)); // ['one','two','three']

// Capturing group keeps the delimiters
console.log('a1b2'.split(/(\d)/)); // ['a','1','b','2','']
```

rx-method-exec-001.explanation:
**Stateful iteration:** a *global* regex remembers a `lastIndex` property. Each `regex.exec(str)` call starts searching from `lastIndex`, returns the next match (a full object with groups and `index`), updates `lastIndex` past it, and finally returns `null` when there are no more — which also resets `lastIndex` to 0.

**The loop idiom:** `while ((m = re.exec(str)) !== null) { ... }` walks through every match, giving you groups and positions each time.

**Pitfalls:** you MUST use the `g` (or `y`) flag, or `lastIndex` never advances and the loop runs forever. And don't share that regex across unrelated calls, since `lastIndex` carries over.

**Modern alternative:** `matchAll` does the same thing without the manual state — prefer it unless you specifically need `exec`.

rx-method-mr-001.explanation:
**Reliable contains-checks:** `/\d/.test(str)` returns a clean boolean, and `str.search(/\d/) !== -1` returns a position you compare to -1. Both are safe and idiomatic.

**Why the others fail:** `str.match(/\d/).length > 0` throws when there's *no* match, because `match` returns `null` (you'd be reading `.length` of `null`). `str.includes(...)` only accepts a *string*, not a regex — passing a regex throws (or stringifies oddly). `str.replace(...)` returns a new string, not a yes/no answer.

**Rule of thumb:** for 'does it match?', reach for `test` first; `search !== -1` is the fallback when you also want the position.

rx-method-lastindex-001.explanation:
**The bug:** a regex with the `g` flag is stateful. `test` (and `exec`) start searching at the regex's `lastIndex` and advance it on each successful match, resetting to 0 only on a *failed* match. Reuse the same global regex across separate `test` calls and the results appear to flip-flop.

**Why true→false→true on `'aa'`:** first call matches at 0, sets `lastIndex` to 1, returns true; second call matches the second `a` at 1, sets `lastIndex` to 2, returns true... actually it depends on the string length — once `lastIndex` passes the end, the next call fails (false) and resets to 0, so it matches again (true). The point: results depend on hidden state.

**The fixes:** (1) don't use `g` for a one-shot boolean test; (2) create a fresh regex each time; (3) reset `re.lastIndex = 0` before each call. A literal regex written inline (`/a/g`) re-evaluates to a *new* object each time, so it's also safe.
rx-method-lastindex-001.example:
```js
const re = /a/g; // shared, stateful
console.log(re.test('aa'), re.lastIndex); // true 1
console.log(re.test('aa'), re.lastIndex); // true 2
console.log(re.test('aa'), re.lastIndex); // false 0 (reset)
console.log(re.test('aa'), re.lastIndex); // true 1 (again!)

// Fix: no g flag for a simple yes/no check
const safe = /a/;
console.log(safe.test('aa'), safe.test('aa')); // true true
```

rx-apply-mcq-001.explanation:
**Anchors make validation work:** `^\d{5}$` means start, exactly five digits, end — so the *entire* string must be a 5-digit code.

**Why the others are wrong:** `/\d{5}/` (no anchors) matches five digits *anywhere*, so it accepts `'abc12345xyz'`. `/^\d+$/` accepts any length of digits, not exactly five. `/[0-9]*/` matches zero-or-more digits and isn't anchored, so it matches practically anything (including an empty string).

**General validation recipe:** decide the exact shape, wrap it in `^...$`, and use precise quantifiers like `{5}` rather than open-ended `+`/`*`.
rx-apply-mcq-001.example:
```js
const isZip = (s) => /^\d{5}$/.test(s);

console.log(isZip('12345'));        // true
console.log(isZip('1234'));         // false (too short)
console.log(isZip('123456'));       // false (too long)
console.log(isZip('abc12345xyz'));  // false (extra chars)

// Without anchors it would wrongly pass:
console.log(/\d{5}/.test('abc12345xyz')); // true (!)
```

rx-apply-001.explanation:
**Extract all words:** `\w+` matches a run of word characters, and the `g` flag makes `match` return every run as an array element. `'hello world foo'.match(/\w+/g)` → `['hello','world','foo']`.

**Why `\w+` over splitting:** `match(/\w+/g)` grabs the words directly and naturally ignores the gaps, so multiple/odd separators and trailing spaces don't produce empty strings. `str.split(/\s+/)` is the alternative when you specifically want to *divide* on whitespace.

**Guard the result:** `match`/g returns `null` if there are no words — use `?? []` if an empty string is possible.

**Tighter words:** `\w` excludes apostrophes/accents; for natural language you might use `[A-Za-z']+` or Unicode property escapes.

rx-apply-mr-001.explanation:
**Goal:** the matched text AND its capture groups, for *every* occurrence. Two tools do this: `matchAll` (spread into an array) and a `while` loop over a global regex's `exec`.

**Why they qualify:** both yield a full match object per occurrence, so `m[0]` plus `m[1]`/`m[2]` and `m.index` are all available for each match.

**Why the others don't:** `match` with `g` returns only the full matched strings and drops the groups. `search` returns a single index. And there is no `String.prototype.test` — `test` is a method of *RegExp*, not String, so `str.test(...)` isn't even valid.

**Recommendation:** prefer `matchAll` — it's declarative and avoids the `lastIndex` state you must manage with the `exec` loop.
